notes.title: How the page appears on Google
notes.text: The blue title and the short description are written by us, and the search phrase comes first in both. The web address carries it too: remindmht.com/vr-therapy-fear-of-heights/. Most people decide from these lines alone.

notes.title: The main headline
notes.text: “Does VR therapy for fear of heights work? It did for Claire”. It asks the one question worried people ask most, and answers it in the same line. It is the first thing anyone who lands here reads, and it tells Google plainly what the page is about.

notes.title: The opening answer
notes.text: The first sentence gives the answer; the next three introduce Claire and say that her fear scores roughly halved. This is the part Google and AI assistants such as ChatGPT are most likely to quote.

notes.title: The search phrase in the section headings
notes.text: The first heading asks “How did VR therapy for fear of heights give Claire her Saturdays back?” and the lines beneath begin the story. The same words come back naturally in a few more headings, never stuffed in, and every heading is a question a reader would actually ask.

notes.title: The picture description
notes.text: Every photograph carries a short written description that Google reads and that a screen reader speaks aloud. This one carries the search phrase as well.

notes.title: A client’s story, with the numbers
notes.text: Before, after and three months on, measured with the questionnaires a clinic would use, plus a chart of every appointment. Worried readers ask one thing above all: does it work? Clear numbers, including the honest “a large improvement, not a disappearance”, persuade where claims cannot. In Claire’s example they are modelled on published VR research.

notes.title: Words in people’s own voices
notes.text: Claire’s own words, Susie’s view of what changed with her name and role beside it (a draft for you to put in your own words), and a real client’s words from a Google review. Quotes in people’s own voices make a story easier to believe. Claire is an example, written to show how a real client story would look and built from published VR research. When a client agrees to share their own story, it takes her place, and the line about changed names stays.

notes.title: Signs of experience and trust
notes.text: Written by Susie Deacon and clinically reviewed by Dr Jane Gilbert, Doctor of Clinical Psychology, with the date, at the top of the page and again at the foot. The page also says plainly what VR therapy cannot do and names the research behind it. Google is careful with health pages and favours ones that a qualified person stands behind.

notes.title: Questions and answers
notes.text: Three questions people ask after reading the story, each answered honestly in a sentence or two. Clear questions with short answers are exactly what Google and AI assistants look for when someone asks a question.

notes.title: Ways to get in touch
notes.text: The form sits at the top of the page and again at the bottom, and your phone number is in the top bar of every page. Nobody has to hunt for it.

notes.title: Links between the pages
notes.text: At the top, the small trail “Home › VR therapy › Case study” leads back to the VR therapy page and the homepage, and the menu and footer do the same on every page. Google follows these links to see how the pages belong together, and a reader who arrives here finds the VR therapy page one click away.

notes.title: Working quietly in the background
notes.text: Behind the scenes, the page carries labels that tell Google what it is: an article, a client story about fear of heights, published by a therapy practice in Whiteley, with the dates it was written and checked. The page also loads quickly on a phone and works for people who use a screen reader or larger text.
